utterance: Hello Mark, I'm Dr. Chen. I understand you've had a cough and fever for a few days and you're feeling quite unwell. Can you tell me more about how this started and what's been going on?
reply: It started three days ago with a dry, hacking cough, and I have been burning up on and off since then, feeling completely roasted even though I do not own a thermometer. Since yesterday, I started bringing things up that went from clear to a rusty, brownish colour, and I also got a sharp pain low down on the right side round towards my back that catches me whenever I take a deep breath or cough.

awards.label: Chest pain with breathing or coughing

utterance: That sounds unpleasant. The rusty sputum and the pain when you breathe in are important. How bad is the pain, and does it stay in that one spot on the right side? Have you felt short of breath, even at rest or when walking around the house?
reply: It is a solid six out of ten when I cough or take a big breath, and otherwise it is just a dull ache staying in that spot. I only get puffed going up the stairs or walking in from the car park, but sitting here I am alright.

utterance: Have you had any shaking chills or sweats with the fever? Any blood in the sputum, or just the rusty colour? And have you had a headache, sore throat, muscle aches, or any tummy symptoms?
reply: Yeah, the first night I was shaking under the doona with my teeth chattering, even though I was boiling. I do not know the word sputum, so what does that mean?

utterance: Sputum just means the phlegm or mucus you cough up. So the rusty brown stuff you mentioned — has there been any bright red blood in it? And have you had a headache, sore throat, aching muscles, or any nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea?
reply: No actual blood, just that rusty colour, and no vomiting either.

awards.label: Red flag excluded: Coughing up blood

utterance: Thanks. Any headache, sore throat, or aching all over? Any feeling sick in the stomach or loose bowels? And has anyone at home or at school been unwell with something similar?
reply: I have not noticed anything like that, and I am not sure about anyone else since I am just trying to get through the end of term with the students.

utterance: Do you smoke, or have you ever smoked? Any history of asthma, lung problems, heart problems, or diabetes? And are you on any regular medicines, including anything from the chemist?
reply: I have never smoked, and I have never had asthma or anything with my lungs or heart problems either. I do not have diabetes, and I am not on any regular medications.

utterance: Have you had any dizziness, confusion, or felt faint? Any pain or burning when you pass urine, or darker urine than usual? And have you travelled overseas recently, or had a flu or COVID vaccine this year?
reply: No, my head is clear, though my wife reckons I am just grumpy, and I have not been anywhere except school and home. I did not get round to the flu jab this year, and I have not noticed anything like urinary symptoms or dizziness.

awards.label: Red flag excluded: Confusion or drowsiness

finding: Flushed and tired-looking. Alert and orientated. Speaking in full sentences. Not cyanosed.
Normal chest shape. Breathing slightly fast; holds back on deep breaths on the right.
Expansion reduced on the right lower chest.
Lungs (front): Resonant. Lungs (back): Dull to percussion at the right base. Left base resonant. Elsewhere: dull at the right base posteriorly. Resonant elsewhere.

Lungs (front): Vesicular breath sounds. No added sounds. Lungs (back): Bronchial breathing with coarse crackles at the right base. Left base clear. Elsewhere: bronchial breathing and coarse crackles at the right base posteriorly. Vesicular elsewhere. No wheeze.
Lungs (front): Normal and symmetrical. Lungs (back): Increased at the right base. Elsewhere: increased at the right base posteriorly. Normal elsewhere.

result: Right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms. Other lobes clear. No pleural effusion. Normal heart size.

utterance: Your examination fits with a chest infection in the lower part of your right lung — that's why it hurts to breathe and why the phlegm looks rusty. I'm going to arrange a chest X-ray to confirm that, and we'll talk about treatment. Are you able to keep fluids down and eat a bit? Is your wife at home to keep an eye on you?
reply: I can keep fluids down and eat a bit. My wife and our two teenagers are at home, and she is working from home this week so she can drive me back in if I need.

awards.label: Who is at home with him

utterance: The X-ray confirms a patch of infection in the bottom of your right lung, called pneumonia. That matches the fever, the rusty phlegm, and the pain when you breathe. Have you ever had a reaction to penicillin or amoxicillin, or any other antibiotic?
reply: Yes, penicillin, because I came up in hives and my lips swelled when I was a kid. It is probably not on my file since I have not needed antibiotics in years.

utterance: Thanks for telling me — hives and swollen lips mean we should avoid penicillin-type antibiotics. Did you have any trouble breathing or a collapse at the time, or was it mainly the rash and lip swelling? And roughly how old were you?
reply: I am not sure about the exact age or the breathing troubles back then, but I just remember the hives and swollen lips.

utterance: We will use a different antibiotic called doxycycline, which is safe with that kind of penicillin reaction. Before I add a pain medicine, have you ever had stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or asthma from anti-inflammatory tablets like ibuprofen or Nurofen?
reply: No, I have not had any of those things.

awards.label: Doxycycline 100 mg orally 12-hourly for 5–7 days (penicillin allergy)
Paracetamol for fever and chest pain

utterance:
Mark, you have pneumonia — a bacterial infection in the lower part of your right lung. The X-ray confirms it, and it explains the fever, the rusty phlegm, and the sharp pain when you breathe or cough. You are well enough to be treated at home, with your wife around.

I've prescribed doxycycline 100 mg, one tablet twice a day for 5 days. Take it with food and a full glass of water, and stay sitting up for half an hour afterwards so it doesn't irritate your gullet. It can make your skin burn more easily in the sun, so use sunscreen and a hat. Don't take it at the same time as antacids, iron, calcium or a big glass of milk — leave a two-hour gap. Please finish all 5 days even if you feel better sooner.

For the fever and the chest pain, take two paracetamol tablets (1 gram) up to every 6 hours, and no more than 8 tablets in a day. I've also given ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food for up to 5 days, which should help the pain when you breathe. Keep drinking fluids, rest, and stay home from school until your fever has gone and you feel clearly better — usually a few days. Cover coughs and wash your hands so you don't pass a virus on, though this pattern is mainly a lung infection rather than a simple cold.

Please come back and see me in 2 days, or sooner if you are not improving. Go to the emergency department — your wife can drive you, or call 000 if you can't — if you become much more short of breath, can't finish a sentence, your lips look blue, you feel faint or confused, the pain gets much worse, you start vomiting and can't keep tablets or fluids down, you cough up fresh blood, or the fever is still high after 48 hours on the antibiotic. I'll also note your penicillin allergy on the file: hives and swollen lips, so penicillin-type antibiotics should be avoided. Any questions about the plan?
reply: Pneumonia sounds pretty serious, and I was hoping I could just shake this off and get back to the kids before the exams next week, but if I need to stay home and take these tablets, I will do it.

utterance: It is a proper chest infection, but yours is the milder kind that usually settles well with tablets at home. Most people start to feel better within two or three days of starting the antibiotic. Don't push back to school before the fever has gone — the exams will still be there, and going back too soon risks you getting worse. Take the first doxycycline dose today with food, and we'll review you in two days. If anything on that warning list happens before then, don't wait — go to emergency.
reply: Right, I understand, and I will get my wife to bring me back in two days or sooner if things get worse.
